theory.title: The Most Specific Route Wins
theory.plainObjective: Three routes all match your destination. Pick the most specific one - the route with the highest prefix number.
theory.summary: Longest-prefix match is one of the most fundamental rules in real networking. Every router on the internet uses it to choose between overlapping routes, millions of times per second.

bodyParagraphs.heading: When multiple rows match - which wins?
bodyParagraphs.text: When a destination IP matches more than one routing table row, the router uses the longest prefix match rule: it always picks the most specific route. A longer prefix length means fewer addresses are covered, so it's a more targeted match.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Prefix lengths and specificity
bodyParagraphs.text: Prefix length measures specificity: /24 covers 256 addresses, /16 covers 65,536, /8 covers 16 million, and /0 covers everything. A longer prefix means fewer addresses - a tighter, more targeted rule.

bodyParagraphs.heading: The default route
bodyParagraphs.text: 0.0.0.0/0 is the catch-all default route. Routers only use it when no more specific rule matches. Real networks use this as a last-resort path to the internet.

theory.mission:
You are 10.1.1.5 delivering to 10.1.1.20.

All three rows at R1 match your destination. Pick the row with the highest prefix number - that is the most specific route.

termIntroductions.headline: CIDR Notation
termIntroductions.body: 10.1.1.0/24 means the first 24 bits identify the network. The /number is the prefix length. Larger number = smaller, more targeted network: /24 covers 256 addresses, /16 covers 65,536.

termIntroductions.headline: Longest Prefix Match
termIntroductions.body: All three routing table entries match 10.1.1.20. Routers always pick the most specific one - the longest prefix. Find the entry with the highest /number and follow that exit.
